claims.text: HfZrTiTa0.53 in the untreated state has a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
HfZrTiTa0.53 in the untreated state has a compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has an approximately 13.5% terminal strain under compression.
The proposed intervention is forging HfZrTiTa0.53 at about 800 °C to 50% thickness reduction followed by annealing at about 1200 °C for 1 hour.
The proposed treatment will produce a refined, partially recrystallized microstructure with a more homogeneous grain-size distribution.
The treatment will introduce a stable dislocation substructure and refine the grain size.
Grain refinement and the dislocation substructure will facilitate dislocation slip and reduce stress concentrations.
The resulting deformation mechanisms will enhance tensile ductility and uniform elongation.
The treated alloy will have tensile uniform elongation greater than 13.5% at room temperature.
The treated alloy will retain a yield strength of at least approximately 786 MPa.
The treatment will not significantly degrade the alloy's impact-triggered chemical-energy release.
Room-temperature quasi-static tension is the principal loading condition for evaluating the predicted ductility improvement.
Matched compression and high-strain-rate impact tests will be used to evaluate retention of compressive and energetic performance.
A previous Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 alloy retained substantial strength and plasticity under dynamic loading at 3000 s−1 and exhibited chemical-energy release.
Excessive grain growth during annealing could undermine alloy strength.
Changes in chemical homogeneity caused by processing could impair impact-triggered energy release.
The treatment effect will be assessed by comparing treated samples with conventionally processed HfZrTiTa0.53 controls.

Failure to obtain statistically significant tensile uniform elongation above 13.5% while maintaining about 786 MPa yield strength, or a noticeable loss of impact energy release, is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% value is initially identified as terminal strain measured in compression, but the baseline calls it tensile ductility or uniform elongation and the prediction and falsification rule use it as the tensile uniform-elongation benchmark. Compressive terminal strain and tensile uniform elongation are not interchangeable measurements.
